question: What recent academic research exists on using machine learning for credit risk assessment?
answer:
## From sources
- A multi-agent framework called Trusted Financial Data (TFD) integrates predictive risk modeling, behavioral intelligence, data-trust assessment, explainable AI, and uncertainty-aware decision orchestration for credit-default and payment-fraud management. [A3]
- Adaptive TFD achieved recall values of 0.6234 and 0.9366, with ROC-AUC values of 0.7584 and 0.9474 on the Home Credit Default Risk and IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection datasets, respectively. [A3]
- A functional representation of credit behavior uses functional data analysis to model probability of default, representing credit variables as continuous-time processes and applying functional logistic regression. [A4]
- Conditional weight of evidence for gradient-boosted credit models measures the change in default log odds from observing a characteristic after the remaining credit information is known, and gradient-boosted trees can estimate this metric accurately. [A2]
- An industrial evaluation program (bakeoff) assessed ten agentic AI platforms on counterparty credit risk, revealing that platform performance can be ranked across nine capability dimensions, with high Cronbach's alpha and strong rank correlations indicating a halo effect. [A1]
- Causal Evidentiary Governance (CEG) introduces a framework for regulated institutions to commit to a versioned directed acyclic graph (DAG) partitioning causal pathways into allowable and disallowed groups, measuring prediction variation attributable to disallowed pathways via the Causal Harm Rate. [A5]

- Caveat: The performance metrics reported are from specific datasets and may not generalize to all credit risk contexts.

sources.title: A Capability Framework for Evaluating Agentic AI Platforms in Regulated Enterprises

sources.title: Conditional Weight of Evidence for Gradient-Boosted Credit Models: Estimation, Additivity and Its Relation to Adverse Action Reasons
sources.text: Traditional weight of evidence assigns a credit characteristic a value based on its association with default across a population. Credit analysis also requires an assessment of that characteristic in the context of an individual applicant's record. We study conditional weight of evidence for this purpose. It measures the change in default log odds from observing a characteristic after the remaining credit information is known. Its sign identifies whether the characteristic adds adverse or favorable information for that applicant, and its magnitude measures the strength of that information. The same characteristic value can therefore receive different assessments for applicants with different payment histories or other credit attributes. We develop estimators using gradient-boosted trees and evaluate their accuracy in a bureau-style simulation. Regressions of the full model's predicted probabilities recover conditional evidence more accurately than separate models fitted to default outcomes, provided the full model is accurate. sources.title: A Functional Representation of Credit Behavior for Probability of Default Modeling
sources.text: This paper proposes a framework for modeling probability of default via functional data analysis. By representing a series of credit variables as functions, we investigate whether intra-monthly information improves default predictability in linear models. We further show how a range of widely used variables, among them available funds, utilization rate, and overdraft, can all be derived from three quantities observed over time. Namely, 1) the type of each account, 2) the balance of the account, and 3) the size of the credit limit on the account. Retaining these quantities as continuous-time processes, rather than reducing them to monthly aggregated values, yields a continuous faithful representation of the borrower. sources.title: Causal Evidentiary Governance for High-Risk Machine Learning Systems
sources.text: Machine learning systems deployed for credit, hiring, and resource distribution are increasingly subject to regulatory oversight from policies such as the EU AI Act and GDPR. Current fairness governance practices rely on observational fairness metrics, post-hoc explainability, and immutable audit logs, but provide limited support for causal attribution and efficient evidentiary verification. We introduce Causal Evidentiary Governance (CEG), a framework in which regulated institutions commit to a versioned directed acyclic graph (DAG) that partitions causal pathways into allowable and disallowed groups. The Causal Harm Rate measures prediction variation attributable to disallowed causal pathways. Each decision is accompanied by a signed Decision-Evidence Packet (DEP), cryptographically binding the prediction to a digest of the published DAG and path-specific attributions. DEP digests can be appended to a Merkle tree to enable logarithmic-cost inclusion proofs. We validate CEG through a two-layer empirical methodology using demographic summaries from four years of PMA credit supervisory data to construct 10,000 synthetic credit applicants across four strategic DAG counterfactuals.
